paper.title: UPPSC GIC Lecturer Mathematics 2026 (14 June)
paper.source: UPPSC Lecturer (Government Inter College) preliminary examination of 14 June 2026, booklet series TUKU-07: part II, Mathematics (questions 41 to 120), as shared after the exam
paper.note: The mathematics part; the whole paper had 40 general-studies and 80 mathematics questions in 2 hours.

en.q: If $\vec r(t)=\begin{cases}2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k, & \text{when } t=2\\ 4\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k, & \text{when } t=3\end{cases}$ then $\int_2^3\left(\vec r\cdot\frac{d\vec r}{dt}\right)dt$ is equal to
en.explanation: $\vec r\cdot\frac{d\vec r}{dt}=\frac12\frac{d}{dt}|\vec r|^2$, so the integral is $\frac12\left[|\vec r|^2\right]_2^3$. Here $|\vec r(3)|^2=16+4+9=29$ and $|\vec r(2)|^2=4+1+4=9$. Value $=\frac12(29-9)=10$.
facts: $\int\vec r\cdot\frac{d\vec r}{dt}\,dt=\frac12|\vec r|^2+C$.

en.q: If F be any field and T be a linear operator on $F^2$ defined by $T(a,b)=(a+b,a)$ then $T^{-1}$ is defined as
en.explanation: Put $T(a,b)=(p,q)$: $a+b=p$ and $a=q$. So $a=q$, $b=p-q$, and $T^{-1}(p,q)=(q,\,p-q)$. Check: $T(q,p-q)=(q+p-q,\,q)=(p,q)$.
facts: To invert a linear map, set $T(a,b)=(p,q)$ and solve for $a,b$.

en.q: If G is any group, then its improper subgroup is/are
en.explanation: Every group $G$ has the two trivial subgroups $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself. In the convention of Indian textbooks (and of these notes) both are called improper subgroups; every other subgroup is proper. The wording 'is/are' and option (c) show the paper uses this convention. (Some books, e.g. Fraleigh, call only $G$ improper and $\{e\}$ the trivial subgroup.)
notes: $\{e\}$ is only one of the two.
$G$ is only one of the two.
The empty set is never a subgroup: it has no identity.
facts: Improper (trivial) subgroups of $G$: $\{e\}$ and $G$.

en.q: If $f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2+1, & 0\le x\le1\\ 3-x, & 1<x\le2\end{cases}$, then Rolle's theorem in $[0,2]$ is
options: Not applicable, because f is discontinuous at $x=1$
en.explanation: $f(0)=1=f(2)$, and $f$ is continuous at 1 ($f(1)=2=\lim_{x\to1^+}(3-x)$). But $Lf'(1)=2$ and $Rf'(1)=-1$, so $f$ is not differentiable at $x=1$ and Rolle's theorem does not apply. (Indeed $f'(x)$ is $2x$ or $-1$ and never vanishes in $(0,2)$.)
notes: Right verdict, wrong reason: $f$ is continuous at $x=1$.
facts: Rolle needs continuity on $[a,b]$, differentiability on $(a,b)$ and $f(a)=f(b)$.

en.q: The equation of the ellipse whose focus is $(-1,1)$, directrix is $x-y+3=0$ and eccentricity is $\frac12$ is given by
notes: Signs of the $xy$, $x$ and $y$ terms are wrong.
Centre at the origin: not this focus.
Centre at the origin: not this focus.
facts: Focus–directrix definition: $SP^2=e^2\,PM^2$, with $PM$ the perpendicular distance to the directrix.

en.q: A bullet of mass m moving with velocity v strikes a block of mass M which is free to move in the direction of motion of the bullet and is embedded in it. What portion of the initial kinetic energy is lost?
en.explanation: Momentum: common velocity $V=\frac{mv}{M+m}$. KE after $=\frac12(M+m)V^2=\frac12mv^2\cdot\frac{m}{M+m}$. So the loss is $\frac12mv^2\left(1-\frac{m}{M+m}\right)$, the fraction $\frac{M}{M+m}$ of the initial KE.
notes: This is the fraction kept, not lost.
facts: Bullet embedded in a free block: fraction of KE lost $=\frac{M}{M+m}$.

en.q: If the spheres $x^2+y^2+z^2-2x-5z+4y=20$ and $x^2+y^2+z^2+2\lambda y-4=0$ cut orthogonally, then the value of $\lambda$ is
facts: Spheres cut orthogonally iff $2(u_1u_2+v_1v_2+w_1w_2)=d_1+d_2$.

en.q: Consider the following statements. I. $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n^2}(2+4+6+\dots+2n)=1$ II. $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n^{16}}(1^{15}+2^{15}+3^{15}+\dots+n^{15})=\frac{1}{16}$ Then
options: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true
en.explanation: I: $2+4+\dots+2n=n(n+1)$ and $\frac{n(n+1)}{n^2}\to1$: true. II: $\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^n\left(\frac rn\right)^{15}\to\int_0^1x^{15}dx=\frac1{16}$: true.
facts: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}\sum_{r=1}^n r^k=\frac{1}{k+1}$.

en.q: If the domain of the function $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3x-22}{2x-19}\right)+\log_e\left(\frac{3x^2-8x+5}{x^2-3x-10}\right)$ is $(\alpha,\beta]$, then the value of $3\alpha+10\beta$ is
en.explanation: $\frac{3x-22}{2x-19}\le1\iff\frac{x-3}{2x-19}\le0\iff3\le x<9.5$, and $\frac{3x-22}{2x-19}\ge-1\iff\frac{5x-41}{2x-19}\ge0\iff x\le8.2$ or $x>9.5$; together $3\le x\le\frac{41}5$. The log needs $\frac{(3x-5)(x-1)}{(x-5)(x+2)}>0$, which on $[3,8.2]$ means $x>5$. Domain $\left(5,\frac{41}5\right]$, so $3\alpha+10\beta=15+82=97$.
facts: Domain of $\sin^{-1}u$: $-1\le u\le1$; of $\log u$: $u>0$. Intersect the two.

en.q: If $f(x)=\log_e\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)$, then $f^{-1}(x)$ is equal to
en.explanation: Let $y=\log(x+\sqrt{1+x^2})$. Then $e^y=x+\sqrt{1+x^2}$ and $e^{-y}=\sqrt{1+x^2}-x$. Subtracting, $x=\frac{e^y-e^{-y}}2$. So $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}2=\sinh x$.
path: 10.10 Inverse circular and inverse hyperbolic functions
facts: $\sinh^{-1}x=\log\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)$.

en.q: If a unit vector $\vec a$ makes an angle $\frac\pi3$ with $\hat i$, $\frac\pi4$ with $\hat j$ and $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ with $\hat k$, then a possible value of $\theta$ is
en.explanation: $\cos^2\frac\pi3+\cos^2\frac\pi4+\cos^2\theta=1$ gives $\frac14+\frac12+\cos^2\theta=1$, so $\cos\theta=\pm\frac12$ and $\theta=\frac\pi3$ or $\frac{2\pi}3$. Only $\frac{2\pi}3$ is offered.
facts: Direction cosines satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.

en.q: The value of the integral $\int_a^b\frac{\sqrt x\,dx}{\sqrt x+\sqrt{a+b-x}}$ is
en.explanation: By $\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)\,dx$, the integral $I$ also equals $\int_a^b\frac{\sqrt{a+b-x}}{\sqrt{a+b-x}+\sqrt x}dx$. Adding, $2I=\int_a^b1\,dx=b-a$, so $I=\frac{b-a}2$.
facts: $\int_a^b\frac{f(x)}{f(x)+f(a+b-x)}dx=\frac{b-a}{2}$.

en.q: Which one of the following are the equations of circles touches the x-axis at a distance 3 from the origin and intercept a distance of 6 on the y-axis?
en.explanation: Take $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$. Touching the x-axis at $(\pm3,0)$: $g=\mp3$ and $c=g^2=9$. The y-intercept $2\sqrt{f^2-c}=6$ gives $f^2=18$, $f=\pm3\sqrt2$. So $x^2+y^2\pm6x\pm6\sqrt2\,y+9=0$ (four circles). Options (c) and (d) list only two of them.
notes: Roles of x and y swapped.
Only the two circles below the x-axis (centres $(\mp3,-3\sqrt2)$).
Only the two circles touching at $(3,0)$.
facts: Chord cut on the y-axis: $2\sqrt{f^2-c}$; touching the x-axis: $g^2=c$.

en.q: An aeroplane is moving with speed 360 km/h. It drops a packet while flying at a height of 980 meters. What will be the horizontal range of the packet? ($g=9.8$ m second$^{-2}$ and $\sqrt2=1.414$)
en.explanation: $u=360$ km/h $=100$ m/s horizontally. Time of fall $t=\sqrt{2h/g}=\sqrt{2\cdot980/9.8}=\sqrt{200}=10\sqrt2$ s. Range $=ut=1000\sqrt2\approx1414$ m.
facts: Packet dropped from a level-flying plane: range $=u\sqrt{2h/g}$.

en.q: Let A be the set of real numbers. Then the relation $R=\{(x,y):xy+1>0\}$ on A is
options: Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
Symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
facts: To disprove transitivity, find $aRb$ and $bRc$ with $a\not Rc$.

en.q: If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are the roots of the equation $x^3+x+1=0$, then the value of $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+3\alpha\beta\gamma$ is
en.explanation: $\sum\alpha=0$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma=-1$. Since $\sum\alpha=0$, $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=3\alpha\beta\gamma=-3$. So the value is $-3+3(-1)=-6$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: If $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$ then $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=3\alpha\beta\gamma$.

en.q: If AB is diameter of the circle $x^2+y^2+2x+4y-3=0$. If co-ordinate of A is $(1,0)$, then co-ordinate of B is
en.explanation: The centre $C=(-1,-2)$ is the mid-point of AB, so $B=2C-A=(-2-1,\,-4-0)=(-3,-4)$.
facts: Other end of a diameter: $B=2C-A$.

en.q: Which of the following relations in the set of real numbers $\mathbb R$ is an equivalence relation?
en.explanation: $|a|=|b|$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (it is equality of $|a|$ and $|b|$). The other three are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric: e.g. $|2|\ge|1|$ but $|1|\not\ge|2|$.
facts: 'Same value of a function', $f(a)=f(b)$, is always an equivalence relation.

en.q: A man is known to speak truth 3 out of 4 times. He throws a die and reports that it is six. Find the probability that is actually six.
en.explanation: Bayes: $P(\text{six}\mid\text{reports six})=\frac{\frac16\cdot\frac34}{\frac16\cdot\frac34+\frac56\cdot\frac14}=\frac{3}{3+5}=\frac38$.
notes: The prior alone; it ignores the report.
facts: Bayes: posterior $=\frac{\text{prior}\times\text{likelihood}}{\sum\text{prior}\times\text{likelihood}}$.

en.q: Solution of $\int\frac{1}{(x^4-1)}dx$ is
en.explanation: $\frac{1}{x^4-1}=\frac12\left(\frac{1}{x^2-1}-\frac{1}{x^2+1}\right)$. With $\int\frac{dx}{x^2-1}=\frac12\log\frac{x-1}{x+1}$, the integral is $\frac14\log\frac{x-1}{x+1}-\frac12\tan^{-1}x+c$.
notes: Log term has the wrong sign.
The $\tan^{-1}$ term has the wrong sign.
facts: $\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}=\frac{1}{2a}\log\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|+c$.

en.q: Foot of perpendicular drawn from one point $(3,2,4)$ to the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ is
en.explanation: A general point of the line is $Q=(3k+2,\,2k+1,\,k+2)$, so $\vec{PQ}=(3k-1,\,2k-1,\,k-2)$. Perpendicular to $(3,2,1)$: $9k-3+4k-2+k-2=0$, so $k=\frac12$. Foot $=\left(\frac72,2,\frac52\right)$.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: Foot of a perpendicular: take the general point Q of the line and solve $\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec d=0$.

en.q: If $(G,*)$ be a group with $x^2=e\ \forall x\in G$, then $(G,*)$ is
en.explanation: Every element is its own inverse, so $ab=(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}=ba$. Hence G is abelian. Option (d) is true as well, but it holds for every group and says nothing about the condition $x^2=e$; the property the condition forces is (b).
notes: Need not be: an infinite product of copies of $\mathbb Z_2$ also has $x^2=e$.
Need not be: $\mathbb Z_2$ is finite.
True of every group, so it says nothing special.
facts: If $x^2=e$ for every x, the group is abelian.

en.q: The generators of a group $G=\{a,a^2,a^3,a^4=e\}$ with multiplication composition are
en.explanation: In a cyclic group of order 4, $a^k$ is a generator iff $\gcd(k,4)=1$, i.e. $k=1,3$. Generators: $a$ and $a^3$.
facts: A cyclic group of order n has $\phi(n)$ generators: $a^k$ with $\gcd(k,n)=1$.

en.q: The eccentricity of the conic $9x^2+4y^2-54x-56y+241=0$ is
en.explanation: Completing squares: $9(x-3)^2+4(y-7)^2=81+196-241=36$, i.e. $\frac{(x-3)^2}{4}+\frac{(y-7)^2}{9}=1$. The major axis is vertical, so $e=\sqrt{1-\frac49}=\frac{\sqrt5}3$.
notes: Greater than 1: impossible for an ellipse.
facts: Ellipse: $e=\sqrt{1-b^2/a^2}$, with $a$ the larger semi-axis.

en.q: If $S_n=\left[\frac{1}{2n}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{4n^2-1}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{4n^2-4}}+\dots+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3n^2+2n-1}}\right]$ then $\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n$ is equal to
en.explanation: The terms are $\frac{1}{\sqrt{4n^2-r^2}}$ for $r=0,1,\dots,n-1$, since $3n^2+2n-1=4n^2-(n-1)^2$. So $S_n=\frac1n\sum\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-(r/n)^2}}\to\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}\frac12=\frac\pi6$.
facts: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum f\left(\frac rn\right)=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$.

en.q: How many triangles can be constructed by connecting the vertices of an octagon so that the triangle have at most one side common with octagon?
en.explanation: All triangles: $\binom83=56$. Those with two sides on the octagon (three consecutive vertices): 8. So $56-8=48$ have at most one common side (32 with exactly one, 16 with none).
notes: Removes the 16 triangles with no common side instead of the 8 with two.
facts: For an n-gon: triangles with exactly one side common $=n(n-4)$; with none $=\frac{n(n-4)(n-5)}{6}$.

en.q: A square is inscribed in the circle $x^2+y^2-10x-6y+30=0$. One side of this square is parallel to $y=x+3$. If $(x_i,y_i)$ are the vertices of the square, then $\sum\left(x_i^2+y_i^2\right)$ is equal to
en.explanation: Centre $(5,3)$, radius 2. The vertices are $(5+2\cos t_i,\,3+2\sin t_i)$ with the $t_i$ a quarter-turn apart, so $\sum\cos t_i=\sum\sin t_i=0$. Then $\sum(x_i^2+y_i^2)=4(25+9+4)+\sum(20\cos t_i+12\sin t_i)=152$. (The direction of the side does not matter.)
facts: For a regular n-gon inscribed in a circle with centre C, radius r: $\sum|P_i|^2=n\left(|C|^2+r^2\right)$.

en.q: If $\vec F=(x^2-yz)\hat i+(y^2-zx)\hat j+(z^2-xy)\hat k$, then the value of $\iiint_V\operatorname{div}\vec F\,dV$, where V is the volume inclosed by the surface $0\le x\le a,\ 0\le y\le b,\ 0\le z\le c$, is
en.explanation: $\operatorname{div}\vec F=2x+2y+2z$. Over the box, $\iiint2x\,dV=a^2bc$, and likewise $ab^2c$ and $abc^2$. Total $=abc(a+b+c)$.
notes: Dimensionally wrong: a volume integral of a length.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: Over the box $[0,a]\times[0,b]\times[0,c]$: $\iiint x\,dV=\frac{a^2}{2}bc$.

en.q: The inequality $\frac{|x|^2-|x|-2}{2|x|-|x|^2-2}>2$ holds if
en.explanation: Put $t=|x|$. The denominator is $-\left((t-1)^2+1\right)<0$, so multiplying by it flips the sign: $t^2-t-2<4t-2t^2-4$, i.e. $3t^2-5t+2<0$, $(3t-2)(t-1)<0$, so $\frac23<|x|<1$.
notes: Includes $x=0$, where the left side is $1$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: Before cross-multiplying an inequality, find the sign of the denominator.

en.q: Under what condition, lines $x=ay+b,\ z=cy+d$ and $x=a'y+b',\ z=c'y+d'$ will be perpendicular to each other?
en.explanation: The first line is $\frac{x-b}{a}=\frac y1=\frac{z-d}{c}$, direction $(a,1,c)$; the second has direction $(a',1,c')$. Perpendicular: $aa'+1+cc'=0$.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: Two lines are perpendicular iff the dot product of their direction ratios is 0.

en.q: The cube roots of $-8i$ are
en.explanation: $-8i=8e^{-i\pi/2}$, so the roots are $2e^{i(-\pi/2+2k\pi)/3}$: $k=0$ gives $2e^{-i\pi/6}=\sqrt3-i$; $k=1$ gives $2e^{i\pi/2}=2i$; $k=2$ gives $2e^{i7\pi/6}=-\sqrt3-i$. Check: $(2i)^3=-8i$.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: The cube roots of z are one root times $1,\omega,\omega^2$, and they add up to 0.

en.q: In how many ways a student can choose 7 subjects out of 10 subjects, if 3 subjects are compulsory?
en.explanation: The 3 compulsory subjects are fixed; choose the other 4 from the remaining 7: $\binom74=35$.
facts: With k items compulsory: $\binom{n-k}{r-k}$ ways.

en.q: Which one of the following definite integrals represent area included between the parabola $4y=3x^2$ and straight line $2y=3x+12$?
en.explanation: They meet where $\frac{3x^2}4=\frac{3x+12}2$: $x^2-2x-8=0$, $x=-2,4$. The line lies above the parabola between them, so the area is $\int_{-2}^4\left(\frac{3x+12}2-\frac34x^2\right)dx\ (=27)$.
facts: Area between curves $=\int(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,dx$ between the intersection points.

en.q: A triangle is formed by the lines $2y-x=5$, $y+2x=7$ and $y-x=1$. Its area is
en.explanation: Vertices: $\left(\frac95,\frac{17}5\right)$ (first and second lines), $(3,4)$ (first and third), $(2,3)$ (second and third). Area $=\frac12\left|\frac95(4-3)+3\left(3-\frac{17}5\right)+2\left(\frac{17}5-4\right)\right|=\frac12\cdot\frac35=\frac3{10}$.

en.q: If $\lim_{x\to0}\left\{\frac{1}{x^8}\left(1-\cos\frac{x^2}{2}-\cos\frac{x^2}{4}+\cos\frac{x^2}{2}\cos\frac{x^2}{4}\right)\right\}=2^{-k}$, then the value of k is
en.explanation: The bracket factors as $\left(1-\cos\frac{x^2}2\right)\left(1-\cos\frac{x^2}4\right)\approx\frac{x^4}{8}\cdot\frac{x^4}{32}$. So the limit is $\frac1{256}=2^{-8}$ and $k=8$.
facts: $1-\cos\theta\approx\frac{\theta^2}{2}$ for small $\theta$.

en.q: Which of the following is NOT a binary operation on the set of integers?
en.explanation: $1\div2=\frac12\notin\mathbb Z$ (and $a\div0$ is undefined), so division is not a binary operation on $\mathbb Z$. Sums, differences and products of integers are integers.
facts: A binary operation on S must send every pair of $S\times S$ into S.

en.q: If C is the curve $z=1,\ x^2+y^2=1$, the value of the integral $\oint_C\left(e^x\,dx+2y\,dy-dz\right)$ is
en.explanation: $e^x\,dx+2y\,dy-dz=d\left(e^x+y^2-z\right)$ is an exact differential (the field $(e^x,2y,-1)$ has zero curl), so its integral round any closed curve is 0.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: The line integral of a gradient field round a closed curve is zero.

en.q: What is the differential equation of all parabolas whose axes are parallel to y-axis?
en.explanation: These parabolas are $y=ax^2+bx+c$ (three constants). Differentiating three times removes them: $\frac{d^3y}{dx^3}=0$.
facts: A family with n arbitrary constants gives a differential equation of order n.

en.q: If a is any element of a group G and $O(a)=30$, then the order of $a^{18}$ will be
notes: This is the gcd, not the order.
facts: If $O(a)=n$ then $O(a^k)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)}$.

en.q: The zero divisors of $\mathbb Z_8$ are
en.explanation: In $\mathbb Z_n$ the non-zero zero divisors are the classes not coprime to n. For $n=8$: $\bar2,\bar4,\bar6$ (e.g. $\bar2\cdot\bar4=\bar0$, $\bar4\cdot\bar6=\bar0$).
facts: In $\mathbb Z_n$, $\bar a\ne\bar0$ is a zero divisor iff $\gcd(a,n)>1$.

en.q: Three like parallel forces P, Q and R act at the corners of a triangle ABC. Their resultant passes through the centroid of the triangle if
en.explanation: The resultant of like parallel forces P, Q, R at A, B, C acts through the point $\frac{P\vec A+Q\vec B+R\vec C}{P+Q+R}$. This is the centroid $\frac{\vec A+\vec B+\vec C}3$ exactly when $P=Q=R$.
notes: Gives the incentre, $\frac{a\vec A+b\vec B+c\vec C}{a+b+c}$.
path: 15.3 Coplanar forces, moments and parallel forces
facts: Like parallel forces P, Q, R at the vertices act through the point with weights $P:Q:R$.

en.q: If $3x+4y=12\sqrt2$ is a tangent to the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1$ for some $a\in\mathbb R$, then the distance between the foci of the ellipse is
en.explanation: The paper prints $\frac{y^2}{a}$, a misprint for $\frac{y^2}{9}$ (as printed no option fits: $a\approx4.84$ and the foci are about 8.62 apart). With $\frac{y^2}{9}$: the line is $y=-\frac34x+3\sqrt2$. Tangency, $c^2=a^2m^2+b^2$: $18=\frac9{16}a^2+9$, so $a^2=16$. Then $a^2e^2=a^2-b^2=7$, and the foci are $2ae=2\sqrt7$ apart.
facts: $y=mx+c$ touches $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ iff $c^2=a^2m^2+b^2$.

en.q: If $|\vec a|=2$, $|\vec b|=5$ and $|\vec a\times\vec b|=8$, then $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ is equal to
en.explanation: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$: $64+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=100$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\pm6$; 6 is offered.
facts: Lagrange's identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$.

en.q: $\lim_{x\to0}\left(\frac{a^x+b^x+c^x}{3}\right)^{2/x}$; $a,b,c>0$; is equal to
en.explanation: A $1^\infty$ form: the limit is $\exp\lim_{x\to0}\frac2x\left(\frac{a^x+b^x+c^x}3-1\right)=\exp\left[\frac23(\log a+\log b+\log c)\right]=(abc)^{2/3}$.
facts: $\lim(1+f)^g=e^{\lim fg}$ when $f\to0$ and $g\to\infty$.

en.q: Value 'a', for which the equations $x^2+ax-1=0$ and $x^2+x+a=0$ have one root in common, is
en.explanation: Subtracting the equations, the common root is $\alpha=\frac{a+1}{a-1}$. Putting it into $x^2+x+a=0$: $(a+1)^2+(a+1)(a-1)+a(a-1)^2=0$, i.e. $a^3+3a=0$. So $a=0$ or $a=\pm i\sqrt3$; of the options only $-i\sqrt3$ works.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: Common root: subtract the equations to get it linearly, then substitute back.

en.q: The plane $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=0$, cuts the cone $yz+zx+xy=0$ in perpendicular generators, if
en.explanation: The plane $ux+vy+wz=0$ cuts $ax^2+by^2+cz^2+2fyz+2gzx+2hxy=0$ in perpendicular generators iff $(b+c)u^2+(c+a)v^2+(a+b)w^2-2fvw-2gwu-2huv=0$. Here $a=b=c=0$ and $f=g=h=\frac12$, giving $-(\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha+\alpha\beta)=0$.
facts: The plane $ux+vy+wz=0$ meets the cone $yz+zx+xy=0$ in perpendicular lines iff $uv+vw+wu=0$.

en.q: Let G be a cyclic group of order 6. Then, the number of elements $g\in G$, such that $G=\langle g\rangle$ is
en.explanation: If $G=\langle a\rangle$ has order 6, then $a^k$ generates G iff $\gcd(k,6)=1$, i.e. $k=1,5$. The number is $\phi(6)=2$.
facts: A cyclic group of order n has $\phi(n)$ generators.

en.q: A body is thrown horizontally from the top of a tower with velocity 20 m/second. It falls on the ground at a distance of 40 m from the foot of the tower. The height of the tower is (Where $g=9.8$ m/sec$^2$)
en.explanation: Time of flight $t=\frac{40}{20}=2$ s. Height $=\frac12gt^2=\frac12(9.8)(4)=19.6$ m.
facts: Horizontal projection: $x=ut$ and $h=\frac12gt^2$.

en.q: Consider the following sets. $A=\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,-1,-2)\}$, $B=\{(0,1,0),(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\}$, $C=\{(1,1,0),(2,1,0),(1,1,0)\}$. Which of the above sets are linearly dependent?
en.explanation: A: $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\1&-1&-2\end{vmatrix}=1(-2+1)-1(0-1)=0$, so A is dependent; indeed $(1,-1,-2)=(1,1,0)-2(0,1,1)$. B: the determinant is $-1\ne0$, independent. C repeats $(1,1,0)$, so it is dependent.
notes: B is independent and A is dependent.
B is independent and C is dependent.
facts: Three vectors of $\mathbb R^3$ are dependent iff their determinant is 0; a repeated vector always makes a set dependent.

en.q: $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are differentiable functions for $0\le x\le1$ such that $f(0)=2$, $g(0)=0$, $f(1)=6$, $g(1)=2$, then there exists a point c satisfying $0<c<1$ and
en.explanation: Cauchy's mean value theorem, in the form $f'(c)\,[g(1)-g(0)]=g'(c)\,[f(1)-f(0)]$: $2f'(c)=4g'(c)$, so $f'(c)=2g'(c)$.
facts: Cauchy MVT: $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)}=\frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}$.

en.q: If A and B are symmetric matrices of the same order, then the matrix $(AB-BA)$ is
en.explanation: $(AB-BA)^T=B^TA^T-A^TB^T=BA-AB=-(AB-BA)$, so it is skew-symmetric.
notes: Only if A and B commute.
facts: For symmetric A and B: $AB+BA$ is symmetric and $AB-BA$ is skew-symmetric.

en.q: Which of the following set of vectors is a basis for vector space $\mathbb R^3$?
en.explanation: With rows $(1,-1,1)$, $(1,0,2)$ and the third vector, the determinants are $-4$ for (a) and 0 for (b), (c), (d). So only (a) is a basis.
facts: n vectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^n$ iff their determinant is non-zero.

en.q: A particle's position is given by $\vec r(t)=2t\hat i+3t^2\hat j$, then the acceleration at $t=1$ is
en.explanation: $\vec v=2\hat i+6t\hat j$ and $\vec a=6\hat j$: magnitude 6 m/s$^2$ at every t, including $t=1$.
facts: Acceleration $=\frac{d^2\vec r}{dt^2}$.

en.q: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. If 3 balls are drawn at random without replacement, then the probability of getting exactly one red ball is
en.explanation: $P=\frac{\binom51\binom32}{\binom83}=\frac{5\cdot3}{56}=\frac{15}{56}$.
path: 16.1 Basic probability and the addition theorem
facts: Drawing without replacement: $P=\frac{\binom{R}{r}\binom{B}{b}}{\binom{N}{n}}$.

en.q: If $f''(x)<0$ for all x in $(a,b)$, then $f'(x)=0$ is
en.explanation: $f''<0$ makes $f'$ strictly decreasing on $(a,b)$, so $f'$ can vanish at most once. It need not vanish at all: e.g. $f(x)=-x^2$ on $(1,2)$.
facts: A strictly monotonic function has at most one zero.

en.q: The greatest height which a particle with initial velocity 'u' can reach on a vertical wall at a distance 'd' from the point of projection is
en.explanation: Height at the wall: $y=d\tan\alpha-\frac{gd^2}{2u^2}(1+\tan^2\alpha)$. This is greatest when $\tan\alpha=\frac{u^2}{gd}$, giving $y=\frac{u^2}g-\frac{gd^2}{2u^2}-\frac{u^2}{2g}=\frac{u^2}{2g}-\frac{gd^2}{2u^2}$.
notes: Exceeds the greatest height $\frac{u^2}{2g}$ of any projectile.
facts: Greatest height on a wall at distance d: $\frac{u^2}{2g}-\frac{gd^2}{2u^2}$ (it is 0 at the maximum range $d=u^2/g$).

en.q: Two operations $\oplus$ and $\otimes$ on the set R of real numbers are defined as follows: $a\oplus b=a+b+1$, $a\otimes b=ab+a+b\ \forall a,b\in R$. The unit elements of the ring $(R,\oplus,\otimes)$ for $\oplus$ and $\otimes$ are respectively
en.explanation: For $\oplus$: $a+e+1=a$ gives $e=-1$. For $\otimes$: $ae+a+e=a$ gives $e(a+1)=0$ for all a, so $e=0$.
facts: Find an identity e from $a*e=a$ for every a.

en.q: If in a group G, $a^5=e$ and $aba^{-1}=b^2$ for all $a,b\in G$. Then for $b\ne e$, $O(b)$ equals to
en.explanation: Read 'for all $a,b$' as 'for some $a,b$' (taken literally, $a=b$ gives $b=b^2$, so $b=e$ and no $b\ne e$ exists). Conjugation respects powers, so $a^2ba^{-2}=a\,b^2\,a^{-1}=(aba^{-1})^2=b^4$, and in general $a^kba^{-k}=b^{2^k}$. With $k=5$ and $a^5=e$: $b=b^{32}$, so $b^{31}=e$. As 31 is prime and $b\ne e$, $O(b)=31$.

en.q: If x, y, z are unequal and $\begin{vmatrix}x&x^2&2+x^3\\y&y^2&2+y^3\\z&z^2&2+z^3\end{vmatrix}=0$, then the value of xyz is
en.explanation: Split the third column: $2\begin{vmatrix}x&x^2&1\\y&y^2&1\\z&z^2&1\end{vmatrix}+xyz\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^2\\1&y&y^2\\1&z&z^2\end{vmatrix}=(2+xyz)(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$. As x, y, z are unequal, $xyz=-2$.
facts: Split a determinant along a column that is a sum; the Vandermonde determinant is non-zero for distinct x, y, z.

en.q: If $\alpha$ is the inclination of the plane to the horizon, $\lambda$ the angle of friction and w the weight of the body, then the least force required to pull the body up the inclined rough plane is
en.explanation: A force P at angle $\theta$ to the plane, with the body about to move up: $P=\frac{w\sin(\alpha+\lambda)}{\cos(\theta-\lambda)}$. This is least when $\theta=\lambda$: $P_{\min}=w\sin(\alpha+\lambda)$.
notes: Least force that just stops the body sliding down.
facts: Least pull up a rough incline: $w\sin(\alpha+\lambda)$, applied at angle $\lambda$ to the plane.

en.q: The sum of first n terms of two arithmetic series are in the ratio $(7n+1):(4n+27)$, then the ratio of their $11^{th}$ terms is
en.explanation: The ratio of the m-th terms equals the ratio of the sums with $n=2m-1$. For $m=11$, $n=21$: $\frac{7(21)+1}{4(21)+27}=\frac{148}{111}=\frac43$.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: For two APs: $\frac{T_m}{T'_m}=\frac{S_{2m-1}}{S'_{2m-1}}$.

en.q: Number of points at which $f(x)=|x^2+x|+|x^2-1|$ is NOT differentiable, is
en.explanation: Candidates: $x=0,-1,1$. At $x=0$: $|x|\,|x+1|$ has a corner. At $x=1$: $|x-1|\,|x+1|$ has a corner. At $x=-1$: $f=|x+1|\left(|x|+|x-1|\right)\approx3|x+1|$, a corner. So 3 points.
facts: $|g(x)|$ has a corner at a simple zero of g; check that two corners do not cancel.

en.q: The length of the normal at the point $(x,y)$ to the curve $y=\frac12a\left(e^{x/a}+e^{-x/a}\right)$ is
en.explanation: $y=a\cosh\frac xa$ and $y'=\sinh\frac xa$. Length of the normal $=y\sqrt{1+y'^2}=a\cosh\frac xa\cdot\cosh\frac xa=a\cosh^2\frac xa\ \left(=\frac{y^2}a\right)$.
facts: Length of the normal $=y\sqrt{1+(dy/dx)^2}$; for the catenary $y=c\cosh\frac xc$ it is $\frac{y^2}{c}$.

en.q: The transverse acceleration at time t of a particle moving in a plane is given by
en.explanation: Transverse acceleration $=\frac1r\frac{d}{dt}\left(r^2\dot\theta\right)=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$.
path: 15.12 Motion in a plane: radial and transverse components
facts: Radial: $\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2$; transverse: $r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$.

en.q: Two spheres of radii 6 and 8 cut orthogonally. The radius of common circle is
en.explanation: Cutting orthogonally, the radii to a common point are perpendicular, so the centres are $\sqrt{36+64}=10$ apart. The common circle's radius is the altitude of this right triangle: $\frac{6\cdot8}{10}=\frac{24}5$.
facts: Orthogonal spheres (or circles): common-circle radius $=\frac{r_1r_2}{\sqrt{r_1^2+r_2^2}}$.

en.q: If a, b, c and d are positive, the value of $\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{a+bx}\right)^{c+dx}$ is
en.explanation: A $1^\infty$ form: the limit is $\exp\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{c+dx}{a+bx}=e^{d/b}$.
notes: The ratio at $x=0$, not at infinity.
facts: $\lim(1+f)^g=e^{\lim fg}$ when $f\to0$ and $g\to\infty$.

en.q: If the equation $x^3+px+q=0$ has two equal roots, then
en.explanation: A double root satisfies $f=0$ and $f'=3x^2+p=0$. Then $x^2=-\frac p3$ and $f=x(x^2+p)+q=\frac{2p}3x+q=0$, so $x=-\frac{3q}{2p}$. Squaring: $\frac{9q^2}{4p^2}=-\frac p3$, i.e. $4p^3+27q^2=0$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $x^3+px+q=0$ has a repeated root iff $4p^3+27q^2=0$.

en.q: The directional derivative of $\delta=xy+yz+zx$ at $(1,2,0)$ in the direction $\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k$ is
en.explanation: $\nabla\delta=(y+z,\ z+x,\ x+y)=(2,1,3)$ at $(1,2,0)$. The unit direction is $\frac13(1,2,2)$. Directional derivative $=\frac{2+2+6}3=\frac{10}3$.
facts: Directional derivative $=\nabla\phi\cdot\hat a$, with $\hat a$ a unit vector.

en.q: If $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are two functions with $g(x)=x+\frac1x$ and $(f\circ g)(x)=x^3+\frac1{x^3}$, then $f'(1)=$
en.explanation: $x^3+\frac1{x^3}=\left(x+\frac1x\right)^3-3\left(x+\frac1x\right)$, so $f(t)=t^3-3t$. Then $f'(t)=3t^2-3$ and $f'(1)=0$. (Strictly, $g(x)=x+\frac1x$ takes only values with $|t|\ge2$, so the data fix f only there; as usual, f is taken to be the polynomial $t^3-3t$.)
facts: $x^3+\frac1{x^3}=t^3-3t$ where $t=x+\frac1x$.

en.q: The set $R=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}$ under addition and multiplication modulo 6 is
en.explanation: $\mathbb Z_6$ is a commutative ring with unity, but $2\cdot3\equiv0\pmod6$. So it has zero divisors and is not an integral domain, a division ring or a field.
facts: $\mathbb Z_n$ is a field iff n is prime.

en.q: In a triangle ABC if $\frac{b+c}{11}=\frac{c+a}{12}=\frac{a+b}{13}$, then the value of $\cos A$ is
en.explanation: Let the common value be k: $b+c=11k$, $c+a=12k$, $a+b=13k$, so $a+b+c=18k$ and $a=7k$, $b=6k$, $c=5k$. $\cos A=\frac{36+25-49}{2\cdot6\cdot5}=\frac{12}{60}=\frac15$.
notes: $\cos A=1$ is impossible in a triangle.
facts: Cosine rule: $\cos A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}$.

en.q: In the group $\{a,a^2,a^3,a^4,a^5,a^6=e\}$, the order of $a^5$ is
en.explanation: The group is cyclic of order 6 and $\gcd(5,6)=1$, so $O(a^5)=\frac{6}{\gcd(6,5)}=6$. (Also $a^5=a^{-1}$, which has the same order as a.)
notes: The exponent is not the order.

en.q: The sum of the infinite series $\frac{1}{1\cdot2\cdot3}+\frac{1}{3\cdot4\cdot5}+\frac{1}{5\cdot6\cdot7}+\dots$ to $\infty$ is
en.explanation: $\frac{1}{(2n-1)2n(2n+1)}=\frac12\left[\left(\frac1{2n-1}-\frac1{2n}\right)-\left(\frac1{2n}-\frac1{2n+1}\right)\right]$. Now $\sum\left(\frac1{2n-1}-\frac1{2n}\right)=\log2$ and $\sum\left(\frac1{2n}-\frac1{2n+1}\right)=1-\log2$. Sum $=\frac12(2\log2-1)=\log2-\frac12$.
notes: Twice the sum: the $\frac12$ is forgotten.
facts: $1-\frac12+\frac13-\frac14+\dots=\log2$.

en.q: For a square matrix A, the value of $(\operatorname{adj}A)^{-1}$ is
en.explanation: For non-singular A, $A\operatorname{adj}A=|A|I$ gives $(\operatorname{adj}A)^{-1}=\frac{A}{|A|}$. Also $\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})=|A^{-1}|\,(A^{-1})^{-1}=\frac{A}{|A|}$. The two are equal.
facts: $(\operatorname{adj}A)^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})=\frac{A}{|A|}$.

path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem

en.q: Let the following vectors $\alpha_1=(1,1,0,1,0,0)$, $\alpha_2=(1,1,0,0,1,0)$, $\alpha_3=(1,1,0,0,0,1)$, $\alpha_4=(1,0,1,1,0,0)$, $\alpha_5=(1,0,1,0,1,0)$, $\alpha_6=(1,0,1,0,0,1)$. The dimension of the vector space spanned by these vectors is
en.explanation: $\alpha_1-\alpha_4=\alpha_2-\alpha_5=\alpha_3-\alpha_6=(0,1,-1,0,0,0)=\varepsilon$, so the span is that of $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\varepsilon$. These four are independent: $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$ differ in the last three places, and only $\varepsilon$ has a non-zero third entry. Dimension 4.
notes: $\alpha_1-\alpha_2-\alpha_4+\alpha_5=0$ and a second such relation cut 6 down to 4.
facts: The dimension of a span equals the rank of the matrix whose rows are the vectors.
